etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English overwerken, possibly from Old English oferwyrċan (“to overwork, overlay”), equivalent to over- +‎ work. Cognate with Dutch overwerken (“to overwork”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make (someone or something) work too hard.

quote.citation: 1945 November snd December, Cecil J. Allen, “British Locomotive Practice and Performance”, in Railway Magazine, page 329:
quote.text: For some years locomotives and coaches have been overworked and undermaintained to a degree without precedent in British railway history, and the leeway in maintenance now to be made up is very great.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fill too full of work; to crowd with labour.

quote.text: My days with toil are overwrought.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English overwerc, from Old English oferweorc, oferġeweorc (“an overwork, superstructure, tomb”), equivalent to over- +‎ work.

quote.citation: 1878, Phosphorus in functional disorders of the nervous system, induced by overwork and other influences incidental to modern life:
quote.text: Various disordered conditions consequent upon overwork, which are characteristic of modern civilisation.

quote.citation: 1946 July and August, K. Westcott Jones, “Isle of Wight Central Railway—2”, in Railway Magazine, page 244:
quote.text: […]  it had obtained from its constituents rather antiquated and inefficient equipment, which scarcely stood up to overwork;  […] .

quote.citation: 1996, Wilkie Au, Urgings of the Heart: A Spirituality of Integration:
quote.text: When it comes to overwork, denial looms large.

quote.citation: 2003, Ernie J Zelinski, Joy of Not Working: A Book for the Retired, Unemployed, and Overworked:
quote.text: The Japanese term for sudden death from overwork.
